The Meet Rule shall not be difficult to obey, especially because
the compiler can give useful feedback.  For example:

%  foo(x:Number, y:ZZ64) = ...
%  foo(x:ZZ64, y:Number) = ...
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{foo}(x\COLONOP\TYP{Number}, y\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = \ldots\)\\
\(  \VAR{foo}(x\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64, y\COLONOP\TYP{Number}) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}

Assuming that \(\hbox{\ZZ64} \prec \hbox{\TYP{Number}}\), the compiler
reports that these two declarations are a problem because of ambiguity
and suggests that a new declaration for \EXP{\VAR{foo}({\ZZ64},
{\ZZ64})} would resolve the ambiguity. As another example, consider:

% bar(x:Printable) = ...
% bar(x:Throwable) = ...
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( \VAR{bar}(x\COLONOP\TYP{Printable}) = \ldots\)\\
\( \VAR{bar}(x\COLONOP\TYP{Throwable}) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}

Assuming that $\hbox{\TYP{Printable}}$ and $\hbox{\TYP{Throwable}}$
are neither comparable by the subtyping relation nor disjoint, the
compiler reports that these two declarations are a problem because
\TYP{Printable} and \TYP{Throwable} are incomparable but possibly
overlapping types.
As a result, these two declarations are statically rejected.

Unlike for functions, the Meet Rule for dotted methods only applies to
dotted methods that are provided by the same trait or object.  This is
possible because two dotted methods are applicable to a given call
$\As_0.f(\As)$ only if they are both provided by the trait or object
$\As_0$.

\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Dotted Methods:}
Suppose that $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are two dotted method
declarations provided by a trait or object $C$ such that neither
$(\Ps_0, \Ps)$ nor $(\Qs_0, \Qs)$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$
and $\Qs$ are not incompatible with one another.
Let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of
types that $\Ps$ defines coercions from and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set
of types that $\Qs$ defines coercions from.
$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and
$\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading if
there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps
\inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$ with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter
\Qs_0)$.

all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps
\inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$ with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter
\Qs_0)$, and
\item
either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or
for all $\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and
$\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
\item
there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ provided by $C$
with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter \Qs_0)$.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

Recall that functional methods can be viewed semantically as top-level
functions, as described in \secref{methods}.  However, treating
functional methods as top-level functions for determining valid
overloading is too restrictive.  In the following example:
\input{\home/advanced/examples/Overloading.tex}
if the functional methods were interpreted as top-level functions then
this program would define two top-level functions with parameter types
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}.
These declarations would be
statically rejected as
an invalid overloading because there is no
relation between \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}; another trait
may extend them both without declaring its own version of the
functional method which may lead to an ambiguous call at run time.
However, notice that declaraions are ambiguous only for calls on
arguments that extend both \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}, and
any type that extends both can include a new declaration that
disambiguates them.  We use this intuition to allow such overloadings.

\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Functional Methods:}
Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two functional method
declarations occurring in trait or object declarations or object expressions
such that neither $\Ps$ nor $\Qs$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
are not incompatible with one another.  Let $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$
have self parameters at $i$ and $j$ respectively.
$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid
overloading if all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$i = j$
\item if there exists a trait or object $C$
that provides both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ then $\Ps \neq \Qs$ and
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provide by $C$
having self parameter at $i$.
\end{itemize}

Also, let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of types that $\Ps$
defines coercions from and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set of types that
$\Qs$ defines coercions from.  $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid
overloading if all of the following hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$i = j$
\item
either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or if there exists a trait or object $C$
that provides both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ then $\Ps \neq \Qs$ and
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provide by $C$, and
\item
either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or
for all $\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and
$\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
\item
there is a declaration $\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ provided by $C$.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

As for functions, where this rule asks for a declaration
$\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$, it is also satisfied by declarations
provided by $C$, having self parameter at $i$, whose parameter types are each a
subtype of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ and together cover $\Ps \inter \Qs$; the case
does not apply to the condition on the types from which $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ define
coercions.
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked here, as for
functions, for a declaration on the intersection itself.}

Notice that the Meet Rule for functional methods requires the self
parameters of two overloaded declarations to be in the same position.
This requirement guarantees that no ambiguity is caused by the
position of the self parameter.  Two declarations which differ in the
position of the self parameter must satisfy either the Subtype Rule or
the Incompatibility Rule to be a valid overloading.

Functional method declarations can overload with function declaraions.
A valid overloading between a functional method declaration and
a function declaration is
determined by applying the (more restrictive) Meet Rule for functions
to both declarations.

\section{Declarations with Static Parameters}
\seclabel{overloading-static-params}

The rules above compare the parameter types and the return types of
declarations without static parameters.
A declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose parameter
type ranges over every instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their
bounds (\secref{overloading-terms}).
A declaration $d_1$ is more specific than a declaration $d_2$ when $d_2$ is
applicable to every call to which $d_1$ is applicable, and not the other way
round (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where neither has static parameters,
this is the relation $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ of the rules above.
A set of overloaded declarations, some or all of which have static parameters,
is a valid overloading when every pair $d_1$, $d_2$ of them satisfies the
following three rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than
the other.
\item
The \emph{Meet Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ exclude each other, or one of them is more
specific than the other, or some declaration of the set is more specific than
both and applicable to every call to which both are applicable.
\item
The \emph{Return Type Rule}: if $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, then for
every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
instance of $d_2$.
\end{itemize}
The Subtype Rule, the Incompatibility Rule and the Meet Rule above are these
rules for declarations without static parameters, with the conditions that
coercion adds; the Return Type Rule is the Subtype Rule's condition on return
types, checked over every instance of the less specific declaration and not
over one instance chosen for the pair.

As in \secref{more-specific-rule}, declarations of the set that are each more
specific than both $d_1$ and $d_2$ and that together cover every argument to
which both are applicable also satisfy the Meet Rule.
\revision{revival-meet}{The type group's paper of 2011 states the Meet Rule
without this case.}

Two parameter types with static parameters exclude each other, for the Meet
Rule and the Incompatibility Rule, as the type group's paper of 2011 decides it
by \emph{existential reduction}: each static parameter stands for any type
within its bound, and where the two parameter types mention one parameterized
trait, instantiation exclusion (\secref{trait-types}) lets them meet only where
the static arguments of those mentions are the same, every static argument but
an operator argument counting.
So where \TYP{Box} and \TYP{Pair} are distinct object types with static
parameters, the parameter types \EXP{\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} and
\EXP{\TYP{Pair}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket} of two declarations exclude each
other whatever \VAR{T}, \VAR{A} and \VAR{B} stand for.
Two parameter types are not taken to exclude each other only because the static
arguments at which they could meet are ones that a bound rules out; declarations
in that case are told apart by an \KWD{excludes} clause or by their names, as
\library\ tell theirs apart.

The Return Type Rule refuses the following pair, where trait \TYP{Round}
extends trait \TYP{Shape} and object \TYP{Circle} extends \TYP{Round}:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident(x: Round): Round = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Round})\COLON \TYP{Round} = x\)
\end{Fortress}
The second declaration is more specific than the first.
For an argument of type \TYP{Circle}, the instance of the first at \TYP{Circle}
is applicable and returns a \TYP{Circle}, but the second, which runs for such an
argument, returns only a \TYP{Round}, and it has no other instance.
The pair is allowed when the second declaration is itself generic:
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Round}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)
\end{Fortress}
Its instance at any type to which it is applicable returns that type.
\revision{revival-overloading}{This section is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 required overloaded declarations to have
identical static parameters and ignored them.
The rules stated are those of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn,
Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple
Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011),
which the compiled type checker applies, with its Return Type Rule checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; the pair refused above has the
shape of that paper's own example, which the compiled path used to accept and
then fail to verify.
The compiled implementation adds one restriction that is not a rule of the
language.
When one declaration with static parameters is more specific than another with
static parameters, the two must declare the same number and kinds of static
parameters of their own, and the return type of the more specific one must be a
subtype of the other's when their static parameters are identified position by
position; for its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration the call dispatches to (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger).
So it refuses this override, whose return type names its static parameters in
the other order, where \TYP{Pr} is an object with two type parameters:
%trait Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\A, B\]
%end
%object M extends Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\B, A\] = Pr[\B, A\](1)
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} M \KWD{extends} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}B, A\rrbracket = \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}B, A\rrbracket(1)\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
The type group's paper of 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019)
instantiates a dispatched declaration from the dynamic types of the arguments
and the static type of the call, renaming static parameters freely
(\secref{resolving-overloading}); under it the override is valid, and the
restriction goes when the compiled dispatcher instantiates a declaration that
way.}

\section{Coercion and Overloading Resolution}
\seclabel{overloading-coercion-resolution}

The overloading rules given in this chapter are
sufficient to prove the following two facts:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If no declaration is applicable to a static call but there is a
declaration that is applicable with coercion then there exists a
single most specific declaration that is applicable with coercion to
the static call.
\item
If any declaration is applicable to a static call then there exists a
single most specific declaration that is applicable to the
corresponding dynamic call and, unless the static type of the argument
stands between a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types
(\secref{more-specific-rule}), a single most specific declaration that is
applicable to the static call.
\end{enumerate}

Moreover, we can prove that the most specific declaration that is
applicable to a dynamic call is the same as or more specific than every
declaration that is applicable to the corresponding static call, so that, by
the Return Type Rule, its return type is a subtype of the return type of each
of them.
Where the declarations applicable to a static call that no other applicable
declaration is more specific than have no static parameters, the type of the
static call is the intersection of their return types; where there is one such
declaration, that is its return type.

\appref{overloaded-functional} formally proves that
the rules discussed in the previous sections guarantee the static resolution of
coercion (described in \secref{resolving-coercion}) is well defined
for functions (the case for methods is analogous).  Also in
\appref{overloaded-functional} is a proof that
the overloading rules for
 function declarations are sufficient to guarantee no
undefined nor ambiguous calls at run time (again,
the case for methods is analogous).
That proof covers declarations without static parameters and calls to which
declarations are applicable without coercion, and it rests on every value of a
trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause being a value of one of its listed types
(\secref{trait-decls}); the appendix states its scope.
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that a single
most specific declaration is applicable to every static call to which any is
applicable, and that the one the dynamic call runs is more specific than it.
With the closed-trait case of the Meet Rule, a static call whose argument's
static type stands between two traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses and their
listed types may have several; the declaration that runs is below every one of
them, and the call's type is the intersection of their return types, which the
Return Type Rule makes sound for declarations without static parameters.
For declarations with static parameters one instance would have to meet every
one of those return types at once, and the type of such a call is not yet
given.
The compiled type checker does not yet enforce across components that every
value of a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is a value of one of its listed
types (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger), which the proof assumes.}

\subsection{Overloading with static parameters}
\seclabel{revival-overloading}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{overloading-terms};
\secref{functional-applicability}; \secref{dotted-method-applicability};
\secref{resolving-overloading}; \secref{principles-overloading};
\secref{overloading-static-params}; \secref{resolving-coercion}; and, in a
draft build, the proposed features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
\item[Change] The sentence of \secref{overloading-terms} that declarations of
one name may not differ in their static parameters, and its echo in
\secref{principles-overloading}, are replaced: declarations of one name may have
different static parameters, or some of them static parameters and others none,
and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose
parameter type ranges over its instances.
Such a declaration is applicable to a call when some instance of it within its
bounds is, and it is compared with others on the parameter types they declare,
taken over all their instances; the static arguments that a call does not write
are inferred for the declaration it selects, after the selection
(\chapref{type-inference}).
The three sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} that inferred static
parameters before applicability was checked and before declarations were
compared, and the chapter's assumption that the static variables of a call have
been instantiated or inferred, are rewritten to match.
A new section, \secref{overloading-static-params}, states for declarations with
static parameters the three rules of the type group's paper of 2011, the No
Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule, the last checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; how two parameter types with
static parameters exclude each other, by existential reduction with
instantiation exclusion; and a pair that the Return Type Rule refuses, in the
shape of that paper's own example, beside the pair that repairs it.
A box in that section states the restriction that the compiled implementation
adds, that of two declarations with static parameters one of which is more
specific than the other the two agree on their static parameters position by
position, with an override that reorders them as its example.
\secref{resolving-coercion} says in three places that a declaration with static
parameters is applicable when some instance of it is, that it is compared on the
parameter types it declares, and that the declaration selected is then
instantiated, the coercions of its instance inserted statically.
In the internal document, the proposed features on relaxing the restrictions on
the static parameters of overloaded functionals and on overloading with static
parameters are marked done, Jan's example answered by \library's factory and the
questions on exclusion by the existential reduction.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 26~September 2026 that the sentence goes and that this working draft states
the model of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick,
Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch
with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 132--180, and

The declaration is chosen first, as \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses it, a
declaration with static parameters being applicable to a call if some instance

is the whole type of parameters takes the narrowest type that their arguments

which every one of them converts, and otherwise the union of their types; every
argument is admitted by substitutability, the coercions the instance needs are
inserted statically, and the converted call dispatches by subtyping.
A call written by tight juxtaposition, as a method invocation or as an operator
application, has an expected type in the contexts the chapter lists, a variable
or field declaration and an assignment to a variable among them, and is
inferred again without it when its result then converts.

\subsection{The Meet Rule for traits with comprises clauses}
\seclabel{revival-meet}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{principles-overloading};
\secref{more-specific-rule}; \secref{overloading-static-params};
\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}; and, in a draft build, the proposed
features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
\item[Change] Where the Meet Rule for functions, or for functional methods,
asks for a declaration on the intersection of two parameter types, declarations
whose parameter types are each a subtype of both and together cover the
intersection also satisfy it, every pair of those declarations satisfying the
rules in turn; the case does not apply to the condition on the types from which
the two parameter types define coercions.
A box at the rule answers the draft note that asks what the intersection of two
declarations is; the Meet Rule of \secref{overloading-static-params} gains the
same case, with a box.
The Meet Rule's example concludes that $V$ covers $S \inter T$, and that $f(V)$
is applicable to and more specific for any call at run time to which $f(S)$ and
$f(T)$ are applicable.
\secref{principles-overloading} says that a static call whose argument's static
type stands between a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types
may have several declarations applicable to it that no other applicable
declaration is more specific than, and is not a static error.
The second of the two facts of \secref{overloading-coercion-resolution} keeps a
single most specific declaration for the dynamic call and, but for such a call,
for the static call; the declaration that the dynamic call runs is the same as
or more specific than every declaration applicable to the static call, its
return type a subtype of theirs; the type of a static call whose most specific
declarations have no static parameters is the intersection of their return
types; and a sentence gives the scope of the proof.
In the internal document, the proposed feature on the intersection of two types
with \KWD{comprises} clauses is marked done.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that the Meet Rule gains the case of declarations that
together cover the intersection, and that a call whose argument's static type
stands between two traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses is typed by the
intersection of its candidates' return types, with the proof of
\appref{overloaded-functional} revised to the uniqueness of the most specific
declaration at run time (\secref{revival-proof}).
The team's list of proposed features records the same plan for the example:
``We agreed to revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check''.
Under the reading of \secref{trait-decls}, the intersection of two traits with
\KWD{comprises} clauses is not in general equal to a named type, and without the
case the Meet Rule would refuse the example given to illustrate it.
The case is an addition to the Meet Rule of the type group's paper of 2011,
which asks for a declaration on the meet, as the type group's calculus
Welterweight Fortress does (\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-meetrule.tick},
in the revival's repository).
The typing of such a call follows from the Return Type Rule: the declaration
that runs is below every most specific declaration of the static call, and its
return type below each of theirs.
For a declaration with static parameters one instance would have to meet every
one of those return types at once, which the proof does not show, so the typing
is stated for declarations without static parameters only.
The covering is a judgement of the overloading rules alone: it makes no type a
subtype of another.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
and \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md} in
the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The Meet Rule's example is valid; both implementations refused it
before this change (row~492 of the revival's gap ledger).
A static call whose argument's static type stands between two traits with
\KWD{comprises} clauses, as an instantiation of a trait with static parameters
that extends both unlisted does, is not a static error: it runs the declaration
that covers its value, and its type is the intersection of the return types of
its most specific declarations.
The Meet Rule for dotted methods keeps its form, asking for a declaration on the
intersection (\secref{revival-notrevised}).
\item[Original text] The Working Draft's rules are unchanged, the cases being
added after them.
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/overloading.tex}, lines 303--307,
the example's conclusion:
\begin{quote}
Because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$.  Thus,
$V = S \inter T$, and the declaration $f(V)$ ``disambiguates'' $f(S)$ and
$f(T)$, i.e., it is applicable to and more specific for any call to which both
$f(S)$ and $f(T)$ are applicable.
\end{quote}
and lines 460--468, the second fact and the sentence after the two:
\begin{quote}
If any declaration is applicable to a static call then there exists a single
most specific declaration that is applicable to the static call and a single
most specific declaration that is applicable to the corresponding dynamic call.

Moreover, we can prove that the most specific declaration that is applicable to
a dynamic call is more specific than the most specific declaration that is
applicable to the corresponding static call.
\end{quote}

#!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
source "$(dirname "$0")/../../../experiment/env.sh"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then
  files=(); for t in "$@"; do files+=("$D/$t"); done
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit, one JVM: $*"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "${files[@]}" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
else
for t in "$@"; do
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit $t"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "$D/$t" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240
  echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
done
fi
clean "$@"

#!/bin/bash
# harness-one.sh <scratch-dir> <file.fss>... : rung C's harness-one.sh (explorations/compile-ladder/
# rung-interp-coercion/, itself rung I's shape): the testSystem harness (SystemJUTest, the class build.xml's
# testSystem shards run) over a directory holding only the named test files, with the JVM settings of

set -u

       -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.tests.unit_tests.SystemJUTest 2>&1 | grep -v '^\s*at ' | sed "s#$FH/##g"

# Climb batch 7b: the gather's record

Written at the gather stage of climb batch 7b (2026-09-30), the second run of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-7.md` (rungs S, C, W and L), on `main` from the base `811053f15`. `main` was at `25cba24fc` when the gather began, seventeen coordinator commits above the base (`161d15135` to `25cba24fc`: boot notes, the cleaning of the landed batches' scratch, the post-mortem's reviews and their fixes, and `POSITIONS.md`'s entry of Pavol's statement on the night's usage limit). None touches a rung's file or anything outside `explorations/`; the ledger, `FACTS.md`, `PLAN.md` and the handover are as the coordinator left them. All four rungs were approved, and each landed as one commit composed from its branch's net change; no branch is a parent of anything on `main`.

**Preconditions.** `811053f15` is an ancestor of `HEAD`, and `git status --porcelain` was empty.

**Scratch.** The gather's patches, tools and probe runs are in its scratchpad, not in the tree. To run the tests it added, the gather built one merged tree outside the main tree: a detached worktree at the base with the four patches applied (`git apply --index`, no conflict), `ant compileAll` (48 s) and the five library components compiled in library order (AnyType 16 s, CompilerBuiltin 71 s, CompilerLibrary 29 s, CompilerAlgebra 1 s, CompilerSystem 2 s). Every harness run quoted below is on that tree, with its own copy of `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh` for `compiler_tests/` and of `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh` for `tests/`.

## The order the rungs were applied in

C, then S, then W, then L. No path is shared by two branches (`git diff --name-only 811053f15...<branch>` for the four, compared: no path in two lists, and the four renames are each one rung's), so the rule of the lowest edited line in a shared file does not order them, and the batch record's own order stands (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-7.md` section 4, "The order the gather applies them": "C, then S, then W, then L"). S follows C because it lands only with C and the gather checks S's text against C's landed tests; W follows S so that its commit carries the correction of S's interpreter callout that W's landing settles; L comes last.

Where one rung's records cite lines another rung's edit moves:
- S's edit and the gather's corrections of it move lines of the specification chapters that C's records cite; C's folded lines cite those passages by name or "at `811053f15`", so none needed re-anchoring.
- C's renamed `ComprisesMeetCompiled.fss` and W's renamed `ComprisesMeetWalk.fss` cite `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`; they are re-anchored in S's commit (C's file) and W's commit (W's file), by the map of unchanged lines, as S's report asks (its section 5).
- No rung's record cites a line of a file that a later rung's edit moves, outside the specification.

## Final row numbers

From 534, the first free row, in manifest order S, C, W, L, each rung's own provisional rows first and then the rows the gather opened from its skeptics' recommendations. Since C lands before S, C's commit appends rows 536 to 546 after row 533 in section 10 of the ledger, and S's commit inserts rows 534 and 535 before them, so that the table stays in numeric order (the precedent is climb batch 7's gather, `compile-ladder/climb-batch-7/RECORD.md`, "Final row numbers"). No row is renumbered.
- S: its provisional 534 keeps its number (walk does not apply the naked-`Any` restriction); its skeptic's first recommended row, the checker's union reaching code generation, is 535.
- C: its provisional rows 534 to 541 are 536 to 543; its second skeptic's recommended rows are 544 (walk runs a type that provides two overlapping functional methods and no cover), 545 (a function beside functional methods, which rule governs) and 546 (the closed-trait case for a family with static parameters).
- W and L: in their sections below.

## Rung C (`rung-return-type-rule`)

**Inherited from the branch.** Fourteen commits, `0d002d8c8` to `91c7b3083`: the tests alone (`0d002d8c8`), the edit and the positional rule's scope (`4ada6fa29`, `f065994f6`), the decision record and the record lines (`837c5bbbb`, `be547b049`, `dbdc68209`); the first skeptic's refusal on D1 (`6545e19c4`); the judge's ruling, repair (`43740c8fb`); the repair round's tests alone, its edit, `REPORT.md` and its corrections (`e2e4d2f32`, `8341b87f5`, `52706eb5b`, `c722be93f`, `e7c5dab6f`); the second skeptic's judgement, approved with three required corrections (`91c7b3083`). `REPORT.md`, `SKEPTIC.md` (both judgements, the second first), `JUDGE.md`, `decision-record.md` and `record.md` were on the branch and stand as they are, with the gather's edits below; no file was written from the journal. The decision record lands with the rung although the gather's rule names one for a specification rung only, since C's FACTS entries and the second skeptic's correction 3 cite it.

**Applied.** `git apply --3way --index` of `git diff --binary 811053f15...wip/rung-return-type-rule` applied without a conflict; its only warnings were whitespace in two captured lines. Every path of the patch matches the branch in the index (blob for blob), the two renames and the deleted `XXXInferLoneBoundUnion.fss` among them.

**Corrections.** The first judgement's eight, which the repair round made, each checked in the file it names:
1. D1: `OverloadingOracle.scala:107-110` substitutes the forced solutions into a kept parameter's bound; `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/OverloadBoundNamesForced.fss` with its `.test` (compile, link, run, `PASS`) asserts `plain` and `generic`; `REPORT.md` section 14 shows it failing on the pre-repair head ("X is not in the kind env") and passing after; `XXXOverloadReturnEveryInstance` and `XXXOverloadPermutedStaticParams` are unchanged.

The rung's tests cite no row number.

**Recommended rows** (the second skeptic's ten; the first judgement's rows are the provisional ones):
- The method call on an intersection-typed result: opened, row 540 (the rung's D2).
- Generic inference on an intersection-typed argument: opened, row 541 (D3).

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the

\(\VAR{printMolecule}(\VAR{molecule}\COLON \TYP{OrganicMolecule}) = \ldots\)\\
\(\VAR{printMolecule}(\VAR{molecule}\COLON \TYP{InorganicMolecule}) = \ldots\)
\end{Fortress}
For the latter, the programmer must provide a
definition for every type listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause of
\TYP{Molecule}, or definitions that together cover those types, or
it is a static error.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked here for a
definition for every immediate subtype of \TYP{Molecule}.
Where a trait with static parameters stands unlisted between a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types, the immediate subtypes and the
listed types differ; the type group's calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012) asks
for definitions for all the types comprised.
The compiled type checker checks the abstract methods of a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause this way; top-level abstract function declarations run on
neither implementation of the revival.}

and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters (\secref{natparams}); the inference
of the static arguments of other kinds of static parameter, and the inference
over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
(\secref{type-inference-components}), are not yet described.
\revision{revival-inference}{The Working Draft of February 2011 left this
chapter a heading and two draft notes, the second of which is kept at its end,
although \chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and
\secref{dotted-method-calls} cite it.
The rule this chapter states is the one the revival decided on 26, 27 and
28~September 2026, and on 29~September 2026 for a lone type parameter with no
narrowest candidate; the compiled type checker was built with this text, and
the cases in which it departs from the text are listed in
\secref{revival-inference}.
The Working Draft had no counterpart to the rule for a numeral whose
conversions tie (\secref{numeral-default}).
A type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause is bounded by
\TYP{Any} (\secref{type-param}); the compiled path still takes \TYP{Object} for
such a parameter of a program's own declarations (row~412 of the revival's gap
ledger).
\chapref{multiple-dispatch} and \chapref{overloaded-declarations} were revised
with this chapter's order, a declaration chosen on the parameter types it
declares and then instantiated (\secref{revival-overloading}).

\revision{revival-overloading}{This section is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 required overloaded declarations to have
identical static parameters and ignored them.
The rules stated are those of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn,
Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple
Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011),
which the compiled type checker applies, with its Return Type Rule checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; the pair refused above has the
shape of that paper's own example, which the compiled path used to accept and
then fail to verify.
Neither implementation runs the pair allowed above today: the interpreter
refuses it at load, since it asks two declarations with static
parameters for a pair of parameter types that exclude each other (row~159 of the
revival's gap ledger), and the compiled code generator fails on it (row~537).
The compiled implementation adds one restriction that is not a rule of the
language.
When one declaration with static parameters is more specific than another that
declares as many static parameters of its own, the two must declare them of the
same kinds, position by position, and the return type of the more specific one
must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are identified
position by position; for its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration the call dispatches to (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger).

the other order, where \TYP{Pr} is an object with two type parameters:

The compiled type checker departs from the chapter in five cases, each gated by
an expected failure of its tests: the expected type can let a declaration
applicable only with coercion be chosen over a declaration with static
parameters that is applicable without it (row~508 of the revival's gap ledger);
a call that the rule instantiates at the bound, with another argument
converted, is refused (row~515); a type parameter declared without an
\KWD{extends} clause, which has no narrowest candidate, is instantiated at the
union of the arguments' types where the chapter gives \TYP{Any} (row~516); and
an argument that is an instance at a union, which only the checker's own union
makes, is refused where it fixes a type parameter (row~518); and an argument
whose static type is an intersection, which the typing of a call between two
traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses gives (\secref{revival-meet}), fixes a type
parameter at one of its conjuncts (row~541).
A written bound, such as \TYP{Number}, is taken by both implementations where
the chapter gives it.
The item of this chapter's list of what it does not yet describe on a static
parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes, and the box on
revival's gap ledger), while the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a
dispatched declaration by substitution and renames static parameters freely
(Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, ``Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with
Variance'', POPL 2019, Sections~4 and~5.2).
That paper's soundness proof excludes an upper bound that names a type
parameter, its own included, and closed types, so that \library's families over a type parameter
bounded by an instance of a trait at itself, such as \STR{SUM}, \STR{BIG~MAX}
and those over \TYP{Integral}, rest on the rules of 2011 as the compiled type
checker implements them, and not on the proof of 2019.
